data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism contains an internal contradiction that dooms its defense independently of the Tichý/Miller objection (already raised). The mechanism explicitly defines corroboration as 'a report of past performance' — purely retrospective, carrying no predictive content. Yet it simultaneously claims that 'Acting on the best-tested theory is the only rational strategy to approximate truth' — a prospective claim about which strategy will get us closer to truth going forward. If corroboration is strictly a report of past performance (as the target states), then the move from 'this theory performed best in past tests' to 'this is the only rational strategy to approximate truth' requires a bridge from past performance to future truth-approximation. The target explicitly denies making 'an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past.' With that bridge removed, corroboration as 'past performance' has zero bearing on which theory will better approximate truth in the future, and the claim that preferring it is 'the only rational strategy' becomes arbitrary: on a genuinely non-inductive reading, any theory — corroborated or not — is equally likely (or unlikely) to approximate truth going forward, since past performance is declared irrelevant to the future. The target cannot simultaneously (a) strip corroboration of all predictive import by calling it a mere report of past performance, (b) deny induction, and (c) claim the preference is 'the only rational strategy to approximate truth.' At least one of these must give way. If (a) and (b) hold, (c) is unsupported. If (c) holds, either (a) or (b) must be false. This is not a gap the verisimilitude mechanism can fill, because verisimilitude is a property of a theory's content, not of its past test performance — and the target's stated justification for the preference is corroboration (past performance), not a direct comparison of truth-content. The target thus smuggles in the very inductive inference it denies.
